Railway rules set the hours: the middle berth can be used for sleeping from 10 pm to 6 am, and must be folded back during the day so the lower berth can be sat on.
explanationWrong: Cleaning isn't the reason. By day, with the middle berth folded up, the lower berth becomes a bench that all three passengers on that side share. Railway rules say the middle berth is for sleeping from 10 pm to 6 am and must be folded back during the day.

The berth is held securely either way. It folds so that by day, the lower berth becomes a bench for all three passengers on that side. Railway rules say the middle berth is for sleeping from 10 pm to 6 am and folded back the rest of the time.

The window isn't the reason. By day, folding the middle berth up turns the lower berth into a bench that all three passengers share. Railway rules say it's for sleeping from 10 pm to 6 am and folded back during the day.

questions.stem: Why is the top pin on an Indian three-pin plug longer and thicker than the other two?
options: It carries most of the power, so it needs more metal to stay cool
Its extra length holds the plug firmly so it can't fall out
It connects to earth first, lets go last, and won't fit a live hole
It was made larger so older, loose sockets could still grip it
questions.hint: Think about which connection you'd want in place before the power arrives.
questions.explanationRight: The big top pin is the earth. Because it's longer, it touches the socket's earth contact before the live and neutral pins connect, and it's the last to leave when you pull the plug out, so a metal-bodied appliance is earthed whenever it has power. Because it's thicker, it can't be pushed into a live or neutral hole by mistake. Indian plugs follow the IS 1293 standard, which is based on the old British BS 546 design.
explanationWrong: The earth pin carries no current in normal use. It's longer so it connects before the live and neutral pins and disconnects after them, keeping a metal appliance earthed whenever it has power, and thicker so it can't go into the wrong hole.

Grip isn't what the length is for. The longer earth pin connects before the live and neutral pins and disconnects after them, so a metal appliance is earthed whenever it has power. Being thicker, it also can't be pushed into the wrong hole.

It isn't about old sockets. The top pin is the earth: longer so it connects before the live and neutral pins and lets go after them, and thicker so it can't be pushed into a live or neutral hole by mistake.
questions.sourceName: Electrical Technology: Why is the earth pin thicker and longer in a 3-pin plug?

questions.stem: Why does the gas from an LPG cooking cylinder smell so strongly of rotten cabbage?
options: The gas starts to break down as it's squeezed into the cylinder
A strong-smelling chemical is added so leaks can't go unnoticed
The smell comes from the rubber pipe reacting with the gas
Natural impurities are left in to keep the price of gas low
questions.hint: Imagine a gas leak you couldn't smell at all.
questions.explanationRight: LPG has no smell of its own. A tiny amount of ethyl mercaptan, a sulphur compound that smells of rotten cabbage, is added so that even a small leak is easy to notice before the gas builds up enough to catch fire or explode. India's oil companies say exactly this in their safety advice: if you smell it, turn off the regulator, open the doors and windows, and don't switch on lights or strike a match.
explanationWrong: LPG doesn't break down in the cylinder; on its own it has no smell at all. A sulphur compound, ethyl mercaptan, is added on purpose so that even a small leak is noticed before the gas can build up and catch fire.

The pipe isn't the source. LPG is odourless, so a strong-smelling sulphur compound, ethyl mercaptan, is added on purpose. That way even a small leak gets noticed before the gas builds up enough to catch fire.

It's the opposite: the gas is odourless, and the smell is added deliberately. A sulphur compound called ethyl mercaptan makes even a small leak easy to notice before the gas can build up and catch fire.
questions.sourceName: ELGAS: The LPG smell of safety

questions.stem: Why is a packet of chips so puffed up with air?
options: It's filled with nitrogen, which keeps chips fresh and stops them breaking
It's a light gas that makes the packets cheaper to transport
Hot air from frying is sealed in and expands as the packet cools
The bag is puffed up so it can survive the pressure on a plane
questions.hint: Think about what makes old chips taste stale, and what happens to a flat packet in a bag.
questions.explanationRight: Chip makers flush the packet with nitrogen before sealing it. Oxygen makes the oil in chips go stale and rancid; nitrogen doesn't react with them, so they stay crisp and fresh for months. The puffed-up packet also works as a cushion, so the chips aren't crushed into crumbs on the way to the shop.
explanationWrong: Nitrogen isn't lighter in any way that matters; it weighs about the same as air. It's there because oxygen makes the oil in chips go stale, and nitrogen doesn't. The puffed-up packet also cushions the chips so they don't break.

Air cools and shrinks, it doesn't expand. The packet is deliberately flushed with nitrogen, because oxygen makes the oil in chips go stale and nitrogen doesn't. The puffed-up bag also cushions the chips on the way to the shop.

Planes aren't the reason. The packet is flushed with nitrogen, because oxygen makes the oil in chips go stale and rancid, and nitrogen doesn't react with them. The puffed-up bag also cushions the chips so they don't break.
questions.sourceName: WITT: How modified atmosphere packaging extends shelf life

questions.stem: Why are most wooden pencils made with six flat sides instead of being round?
options: Six sides make the pencil much harder to snap in half
The flat faces were added to print the maker's name clearly
Flat sides stop them rolling off a desk and give fingers a grip
The sides hide the seam where the two wooden halves are glued
questions.hint: Put a round pen down on a slightly sloping desk.
questions.explanationRight: A round pencil rolls off any desk that isn't perfectly level. Six flat sides stop that, and the edges give the fingers something to hold. There's a maker's reason too: a hexagon wastes less of the wooden slat than a circle, so the same slat can be cut into more pencils.
explanationWrong: A hexagon isn't meaningfully stronger. The flat sides are there so the pencil doesn't roll off a desk, and so fingers can grip it. Makers liked it too: a hexagon wastes less of the wooden slat, so each slat gives more pencils.
Round pencils are printed on just fine. The flat sides are there so the pencil doesn't roll off a desk and is easy to grip, and a hexagon wastes less wood, so each wooden slat makes more pencils.
The shape doesn't hide the glued seam. The flat sides stop the pencil rolling off a desk and give fingers a grip, and a hexagon wastes less of the wooden slat, so each slat makes more pencils.
questions.sourceName: IFLScience: Why are pencils hexagonal?

questions.stem: Why do many padlocks have a tiny hole in the bottom of the body?
options: It lets rainwater drain out so the lock doesn't rust or freeze
It's where the factory tested the lock by pushing a pin through it
It lets the owner tie the lock to a chain so it can't get lost
It lets air in so the shackle doesn't stick when it's cold
questions.hint: Picture a padlock left on a gate through a rainy winter.
questions.explanationRight: Padlocks spend their lives outdoors, and water gets in around the shackle and keyhole. The small hole at the bottom lets it drain out instead of pooling inside, where it would rust the pins and springs, or freeze and jam the mechanism in cold weather. The same hole is a handy spot to add a little lubricant.
explanationWrong: It isn't a factory leftover. The hole lets water that gets into the lock drain out instead of pooling inside, where it would rust the mechanism or freeze solid in cold weather. It also makes a handy spot to add lubricant.
It's too small for a chain. The hole is a drain: water that gets in around the shackle and keyhole runs out instead of pooling inside, where it would rust the parts or freeze and jam the lock.
It's about water, not air. Rain gets in around the shackle and keyhole, and the hole lets it drain out rather than pool inside, where it would rust the parts or freeze and jam the lock in winter.
questions.sourceName: Monroe Engineering: Why padlocks have a small hole on the bottom

questions.stem: Why do some car side mirrors warn that objects are closer than they appear?
options: The mirror bulges outward to show a wider view, which shrinks things
The glass is tinted to cut glare, which makes things look far off
The mirror sits far from the driver's eyes, so everything looks small
Cheap glass bends the light, and makers are required to admit it
questions.hint: Compare your reflection in a flat mirror with the back of a spoon.
questions.explanationRight: The passenger-side mirror is convex: it bulges outward, like the back of a spoon. That shows a much wider view, which helps cover the blind spot beside the car, but everything in it looks smaller, and smaller things look further away. The driver's-side mirror is flat, showing true distances but a narrower view. US federal rules require the convex mirror to carry the warning printed on the glass.
explanationWrong: Tint isn't the reason. The mirror is convex, bulging outward like the back of a spoon, so it shows a wider view that helps cover the blind spot. The catch is that everything looks smaller, so it seems further away.

Distance from the eye isn't it. The mirror is convex, bulging outward like the back of a spoon, so it shows a wider view that helps cover the blind spot, but makes everything look smaller and so further away.

The glass is fine; the curve is deliberate. The mirror bulges outward like the back of a spoon, giving a wider view that helps cover the blind spot, at the cost of making things look smaller and further away.
questions.sourceName: US Code of Federal Regulations: FMVSS 111, rearview mirrors

tidbits.text: A kingfisher can dive from the air into a river at full speed and barely leave a splash. Its long, narrow beak eases into the water instead of slamming into it. Engineers who build very fast things, especially things that plunge into tight spaces, have taken notes.

Railway networks used to keep all their station clocks in step with one master clock, which sent out an electrical pulse at the start of every minute. A clock that ran a little fast didn't need fixing. It just had to wait for the pulse.

Car suspension works by letting springs carry weight and push back just as hard as they are pushed, so the body floats steady over bumps. In the early 1930s, one suspension engineer started wondering what else a set of well chosen springs could hold perfectly still.

Air always tries to move from high pressure to low. Under a flying wing the pressure is higher than on top, so right at the tip, air curls round from underneath and spins away behind the plane in a long, invisible swirl that tugs it backwards.

In the 1800s, shipping furniture across oceans was expensive, and much of that cost was paying to move empty space. A chair in pieces takes up a small fraction of the room of a built one. One Viennese company worked out that 36 of theirs fitted in a single cubic metre.

Next time you're in a busy café, glance under the tables. Table legs, chair legs, people's legs, all crossing each other. One well known designer found that view so messy that he called it a slum, and spent years trying to get rid of it.

Sit on a foam cushion for a few hours and the patch under you gets warm and a little damp. Foam holds heat and moisture close to the skin, while an open weave lets both drift away. Office chair makers have spent a lot of money on that difference.

On an underground train there's nothing to see out of the window but tunnel wall. What riders really keep track of is how many stops are left and where they need to change. How far apart those stops are hardly matters.

Before push button phones reached homes, Bell Labs asked volunteers to try out many different arrangements of number keys. The researchers timed them, counted mistakes, and asked which layouts felt most natural. Most people liked numbers that ran the way they read.

On the early Macintosh, every keyboard shortcut in the menus was shown with a tiny apple beside it. Open a long menu and you'd see a whole column of little logos. Not everyone at Apple thought that was a good look.
A touchscreen can't tell a finger from the lining of a pocket. Anything that presses on it counts as a touch, which is why phone makers need a way for the phone to know you really mean it.

In the early 1900s, shop shelves were full of drinks with names like Koka-Nola and Toka-Cola, dressed up to look like the famous brand. The real one needed a way to be spotted instantly, even without looking.

Yellow with black on top is one of the easiest colour pairs to pick out, which is why it turns up on so many warning signs. Now picture the grey half light of a winter morning, when children are waiting at the side of the road.

In the 1920s, some American road planners wanted sign shapes to speak for themselves. Their idea: the more corners a sign had, the more careful you should be. A circle, with no corners at all, counted as having endless sides.
